questions.prompt: What does ä represent?
questions.answer: An umlauted a; its common short sound is similar to [ɛ], while its exact quality depends on length and context.
questions.explanation: This card follows standard German pronunciation and spelling conventions; IPA gives a more precise description than an English sound analogy.

questions.prompt: What does ö represent?
questions.answer: An umlauted o; round the lips for an o while producing a front vowel.
questions.explanation: This card follows standard German pronunciation and spelling conventions; IPA gives a more precise description than an English sound analogy.

questions.prompt: What does ü represent?
questions.answer: An umlauted u; round the lips as for u while keeping the tongue position closer to i.
questions.explanation: This card follows standard German pronunciation and spelling conventions; IPA gives a more precise description than an English sound analogy.

questions.prompt: What is ß called in German?
questions.answer: Eszett or scharfes S; it represents an s sound and is not a separate vowel.
questions.explanation: This card follows standard German pronunciation and spelling conventions; IPA gives a more precise description than an English sound analogy.

questions.prompt: How is ß normally written in Swiss Standard German?

questions.prompt: How is ch pronounced after i, e, ä, ö, ü and many consonants?

questions.prompt: How is ch pronounced after a, o, u and au?

questions.explanation: In standard German, z commonly represents the affricate [ts], as in Zeit.

questions.prompt: Capitalized Sie can be formal “you.”
questions.explanation: Sie is the formal second-person pronoun and is always capitalized in this use.

questions.prompt: “Morgen” can mean both “morning” and “tomorrow.”
questions.explanation: The noun der Morgen means morning, while morgen as an adverb means tomorrow.

questions.prompt: A German yes/no question normally begins with the subject.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question normally begins with the finite verb: Kommst du?

questions.prompt: “Bitte” can mean “please” and “you’re welcome.”
questions.explanation: Context determines whether Bitte introduces a request or replies to Danke.

questions.prompt: German uses a comma in place of a decimal point in standard number writing.
questions.explanation: German standard number writing uses a comma for decimals, as in 3,5; local conventions should be followed in technical contexts.

questions.prompt: The ß character is pronounced like the English letter name “B.”
questions.explanation: ß represents an s sound and is called Eszett or scharfes S.
